info.title: SyteCheck API
info.description:
The SyteCheck public API runs comprehensive, scored audits of any website —
SEO, accessibility, performance, security headers, and more.

## Authentication

All `/api/v1` routes accept either a session JWT or a personal **API key** via the
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. Generate API keys from your account settings
or the `POST /api/v1/keys` endpoint. See the getting-started guide in `docs/PUBLIC_API.md`.

## Plans and quotas

Every account has a monthly scan quota, a set of analysis categories, and a concurrency
limit set by its plan. **The API itself is available on every plan, including Free** —
an API key confers no allowance of its own, reaching the same quota and the same
categories as the plan it belongs to. Exceeding the
monthly quota returns `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header giving the
time until the calendar month rolls over. Requesting a category your plan does not
include returns `403 Forbidden`. A separate daily burst cap also applies as abuse and
infrastructure protection. See `docs/PUBLIC_API.md` for the current limits.

## Webhooks

Pass a `webhook_url` when submitting a scan to receive the completed result payload
by HTTP POST as soon as analysis finishes; delivery is retried on failure. Webhooks
require the **Agency** plan — on any other plan the field is refused with `403` and
the scan should be submitted without it, then polled or streamed for completion.

get.description: Return service health. Checks DB connectivity.
Return non-secret runtime configuration for the web UI.

post.description:
Set a new password from a reset token, and confirm the address while at it.

Redeeming a link mailed to an address is proof of control over it, which is
exactly what verification asserts — the same reasoning already applied to Google
sign-in. Without the stamp, an unverified account that resets its password lands
in a dead end: a working sign-in whose every scan is refused, and no verification
link in flight. An already-verified stamp is left alone.

Take possession of an admin-created account: set its first password.

Redeeming the link also stamps ``email_verified_at`` — the link was mailed to
the address, so clicking it proves control of it — and signs the invitee in. The
account has never had a session, so there is none to invalidate, and asking for
the password again immediately after setting it is friction with no security
value.

Unknown, expired, and already-used tokens all answer with the *same* 400: the
endpoint takes a secret and nothing else, so it must never become a way to learn
which addresses have accounts.

A disabled account is refused with 403 and the token is left unused, so
re-enabling makes the same link work again — that is the recovery path after an
invitation is revoked by mistake. Setting a password on an account that already
has one is deliberately allowed: possession of the mailed link is exactly the
standard password reset runs on, and refusing would strand someone who used the
reset flow first.

Confirm an email address from a verification token.

Serves both verification flows. A token with no ``new_email`` confirms the
address the account already has: it marks the token used and stamps
``email_verified_at``, and re-verifying an already-verified account is a no-op
success so the link stays idempotent.

A token carrying a ``new_email`` is the second half of an address change — this
is the point at which ``users.email`` actually moves, and the verified stamp is
refreshed because it now describes a newly proved address. Uniqueness is
re-checked here and not only at request time: the token is valid for 24 hours,
during which someone else may have registered the address.

A token that is unknown, already used, or expired is rejected with 400.

Re-send the verification link to the authenticated user's email.

Requires authentication (an unverified user can still sign in), which avoids
the email-enumeration concern of the by-email password-reset flow. Already-
verified accounts short-circuit without sending another email.

Begin moving the account to a different email address.

Deliberately returns **202, not 200**: nothing has changed yet. A confirmation
link goes to the new address and ``users.email`` moves only when it is clicked
(``POST /auth/verify-email``). Verifying before applying is what keeps a typo
from stranding an account on an inbox its owner cannot reach — password-reset
and every other recovery path would follow the bad address — and stops an
account from ever pointing at an address its owner does not control.

Re-authenticates first, mirroring ``POST /auth/change-password``. A live
session is not enough on its own: the confirmation link goes to the address
the requester named, so whoever holds a stolen session would receive it, and
from a changed address every recovery path — password reset included — belongs
to them. Accounts that sign in with Google have no password to re-enter and
skip this; their recovery path is Google's, not ours.

Rate-limited per hour rather than per minute: each call also mails the current
address, and that notice must not become a way to flood someone's inbox.
Change the authenticated user's password after verifying the current one.

Verify a Google ID token and return a JWT pair.

Finds an existing account by google_id, falls back to matching by email
(linking a pre-existing password account), or creates a new account.

delete.description:
Permanently erase the caller's account and all associated data (GDPR/CCPA).

Unlike the soft-delete used for individual scans, this is an immediate, irreversible
hard delete: the user row is removed and the ``ondelete="CASCADE"`` foreign keys on
scans (and, transitively, their results and screenshots), API keys, and auth tokens
cascade-remove every associated row — which also neutralizes any live session or key.
The screenshots' object-storage blobs are cleaned up asynchronously afterwards.

An account that performed admin actions is refused (409): those actions are recorded
in the append-only audit log under a ``RESTRICT`` foreign key that must not be
orphaned. Such an account has to be handled by another administrator.

An account with a live subscription is also refused (409). Erasure removes our
record of the subscription but not Paddle's, which would keep billing a customer
for a plan whose account no longer exists — so Privacy Policy §7 tells them to
cancel first, and this enforces what it says.

patch.description:
Update the caller's profile.

Email is not settable here. Changing an address has to prove the new one is
reachable first, which is a two-step flow this single-shot PATCH cannot
express, so it lives at ``POST /auth/change-email``. The field is still
accepted and rejected explicitly rather than dropped from the schema, so a
client that was setting it gets told where the flow moved instead of watching
the write silently do nothing.

get.description:
Return the caller's plan entitlements and their usage against them.

Kept off ``GET /users/me`` deliberately: that endpoint is polled by the SPA
on every page and is a single row read, whereas this one runs a COUNT over
the caller's scans for the current calendar month.

Return the caller's webhook signing secret, deriving it on demand.

Readable repeatedly, unlike an API key. The secret is not a bearer credential
— it verifies that a delivery came from us and grants access to nothing — so
the cost of re-showing it is low, while forcing a rotation to recover a lost
value would break a working integration for no security gain.

Gated on the `webhooks` entitlement rather than `public_api`: an account that
cannot register a webhook has nothing to verify, and handing out a secret for
a feature the plan does not include only invites a support question.

post.description:
Issue a new signing secret for the caller, invalidating the previous one.

Bumping `webhook_secret_version` re-derives the secret for this account alone.
There is deliberately **no overlap window**: the old secret stops being valid
the moment this returns, so a receiver must be updated first. A grace period
would mean signing each delivery twice or accepting either secret, which is
exactly the ambiguity a customer rotates to *remove* after a leak.

get.description:
Return the analysis categories, each flagged with the caller's access.

Every category is always listed — the SPA's picker renders the withheld ones
as locked rather than hiding them, so a free user can see what upgrading
buys. Authentication is required (Phase 11 B3): the response is now
per-account, and scanning already requires a registered, verified account,
so there is nothing an anonymous caller could do with it.

Return a paginated list of the authenticated user's scans, newest first.

Optionally narrowed by a free-text search (`q`, matched against URL and label)
and/or an exact `status` filter.

post.description:
Submit a URL for analysis.

Validates the requested categories, enforces every plan entitlement that
applies at submission time (category access, monthly scan quota, webhook
access, concurrency, and the daily burst cap), persists a scan record, and
enqueues the Celery job. Returns immediately with the scan ID and status
"queued".

The checks run cheapest-and-most-explanatory first: a caller who is both
unverified and out of quota should hear about verification, and a caller
asking for a category their plan lacks should be told that rather than being
silently charged a scan against their quota.

schema.description: Language for report content (e.g. 'es', 'pt-BR'). Falls back to the Accept-Language header, then English.
schema.title: Lang

parameters.description: Language for report content (e.g. 'es', 'pt-BR'). Falls back to the Accept-Language header, then English.

get.description:
Return per-URL overall-score history for the caller's completed scans.

Powers the dashboard trend chart and the scan-history sparklines. Points are
ordered oldest-first and capped at the most recent ``_MAX_TREND_POINTS_PER_URL``
per URL.

Report whether the caller scanned this website within the warning window.

Advisory pre-submit check: lets the web UI caution the user against re-scanning
a site they scanned recently (which can trip the site's WAF). Scoped to the
caller's own scans; never blocks submission.

schema.description: The URL about to be scanned.

parameters.description: The URL about to be scanned.

get.description: Return the current status and results for a scan owned by the caller.

patch.description:
Update the editable fields of a scan owned by the caller (currently the label).

Only fields explicitly present in the request body are applied, so an empty
PATCH is a no-op rather than clearing the label. Sending ``{"label": null}``
still clears it (the key is present). This keeps PATCH semantics correct and
avoids the partial-update clobber if more editable fields are added later.

delete.description:
Soft-delete a scan owned by the caller.

Sets ``deleted_at`` so the scan is hidden from every listing and lookup
(all read queries filter ``deleted_at IS NULL``) while its results and
screenshots are preserved during a grace window. The Phase 11 retention purge
(worker/tasks/retention.py) permanently removes the row and its object-storage
screenshots ``retention_soft_delete_purge_days`` after this soft delete.

get.description:
Return the full structured report for a completed scan.

Parses raw analyzer results into structured findings and generates
pre-signed URLs for all screenshots. The report's free text (findings,
summaries) is translated into the requested language; English content is
canonical and is returned unchanged when ``lang`` is English.

parameters.name: lang

schema.description: Language for report content (e.g. 'es', 'pt-BR'). Falls back to the Accept-Language header, then English.
schema.title: Lang

parameters.description: Language for report content (e.g. 'es', 'pt-BR'). Falls back to the Accept-Language header, then English.

get.description:
Generate and return a PDF version of the scan report.

Both the report's free text (findings, summaries) and its static chrome
(headings, labels) are localized to the requested language.

PDF export is a paid entitlement (Phase 11 B3) — the client-ready PDF is
precisely the freelance deliverable, so the free plan gets the on-screen
report only.

parameters.name: lang

schema.description: Language for report content (e.g. 'es', 'pt-BR'). Falls back to the Accept-Language header, then English.

parameters.description: Language for report content (e.g. 'es', 'pt-BR'). Falls back to the Accept-Language header, then English.

get.description:
Stream real-time scan status updates using Server-Sent Events.

Yields a `status` event each time the scan's status changes, and a final
`done` event when the scan reaches a terminal state (complete or failed).
Times out after 5 minutes with a `timeout` event if the scan hasn't finished.
Return all of the caller's API keys (active and revoked), newest first.

post.description:
Generate a new API key for the caller.

The raw secret is included in this response only and is never retrievable
again — store it securely on receipt.

Every tier may mint a key (opened up on 2026-09-09). The `public_api` check
below therefore refuses nothing today, and is kept as the mechanism for any
future tier that withholds programmatic access. A key grants no allowance of
its own: it reaches the same monthly quota and the same category set the
account already has. Webhooks are the separate `webhooks` entitlement and
remain Agency-only — that check lives on scan creation.

Existing keys on a downgraded account stop authenticating via the matching
check in :mod:`api.dependencies`, the one place the owning user is loaded on
every keyed request.

delete.description: Revoke an API key. Revocation is permanent; the key stops working at once.

get.description:
Return every plan, including Free, for the public pricing page.

Two things about this route are deliberate and easy to mistake for oversights.

**It takes no authentication.** Every other route in this router declares
`Depends(get_current_user_id)` individually — there is no router-level
dependency — so the omission here is a single missing line and is stated
explicitly for that reason. It is the pricing page's data source, and that
page is read by people who have no account yet; nothing returned is
account-specific.

**It is not behind `_require_billing_enabled()`.** With no Paddle catalog
configured the page must still publish the plan matrix in USD; it simply
cannot offer a localized price. So this mirrors `GET /api/v1/config`, which
withholds the client token rather than failing: `billing_enabled` is reported
honestly and the price ids come back null.

`PLANS` stays the single source, so the published page cannot drift from
`docs/product/COST_AND_PRICING.md` §2.3 without failing a test.

Return the caller's plan, subscription state, and audit-credit balance.

Deliberately separate from ``GET /users/me/usage``: that endpoint is the
quota surface and already runs a COUNT, and this one is read only on the
billing page.

post.description:
Create a Paddle transaction for the browser's checkout overlay.

Server-side on purpose. Creating the transaction here is what makes the
account id in `custom_data` trustworthy: the browser only ever receives an
opaque transaction id, so it cannot nominate whose account a payment credits.

A **verified email is a hard prerequisite** — B2 made the free tier the trial
and made verification the gate in its place, and an unverified buyer is a
chargeback and a support ticket waiting to happen.

get.description:
Mint short-lived authenticated links into Paddle's customer portal.

This is where invoice history and payment-method updates live. Building those
ourselves would mean handling payment data we have published that we never
receive, so they stay Paddle's.

post.description:
Move the caller's subscription to a different plan or billing period.

Both directions take effect immediately and are prorated, which is what ToS §9
publishes. Upgrades bill the difference now; downgrades credit the unused
remainder against the next invoice. The symmetry is not a simplification — it
is forced, because Paddle applies every item change at once and can only defer
the *billing* (see `change_subscription_price`).

Paddle then reports the resulting state back through `subscription.updated`,
which is what actually moves the tier. This response is therefore usually one
step behind; the SPA polls.

Cancel at the end of the current billing period, per ToS §9.

Not immediate, and not prorated — the customer has paid for this period and
keeps it. Paddle sends `subscription.canceled` when it actually takes effect,
which is what drops the tier; nothing here needs a scheduler.

Exercise the EU/UK 14-day right of withdrawal.

Directive (EU) 2023/2673 Art. 11a requires a prominent control available
throughout the withdrawal period; ToS §9 has published that it lives on the
account billing page. Unlike cancellation this unwinds the contract rather
than letting it run out: the subscription ends immediately *and* everything
paid inside the window is refunded.

The two halves are independent on purpose. Cancelling stops future billing;
refunding returns money already taken, and it is the half the Directive
actually compels — so a failure to cancel must not skip it.

**A Paddle failure must not cost the customer the right.** Whatever fails is
logged at ERROR for manual completion and the caller is told the withdrawal
was received, rather than being handed a 500 and left to wonder.

Scopes never widen what a key can reach: account, billing, and key-management routes are closed to every key.

current_password.description: The account's current password. Required unless the account signs in with Google and has no password set.

ChangeEmailRequest.title: ChangeEmailRequest
ChangeEmailRequest.description:
Request to move the account to a different email address.

The address is not applied here — a confirmation link is sent to it, and only
clicking that link updates the account (see ``POST /auth/change-email``).

CheckoutRequest.title: CheckoutRequest
CheckoutRequest.description:
What the customer wants to buy.

Either a subscription (`plan` + `period`) or the one-off audit
(`product="one_off_scan"`). Prices are never sent by the client — the server
resolves the Paddle price id from the plan table, so a tampered request buys
nothing unexpected.

CheckoutResponse.title: CheckoutResponse
CheckoutResponse.description:
A Paddle transaction to hand to `Paddle.Checkout.open({ transactionId })`.

The browser gets only this opaque id. The account the payment credits is set
server-side in the transaction's `custom_data`, so it cannot be nominated by
the client.

ExecutiveSummary.title: ExecutiveSummary
ExecutiveSummary.description: Claude-generated plain-English overview and prioritised actions for a scan.

FindingResponse.title: FindingResponse
FindingResponse.description: One finding within a category report.

MetricReport.title: MetricReport
MetricReport.description:
One measured metric within a category report.

Distinct from a finding: a finding is something to fix, a metric is simply
something measured. A category can report metrics with no findings at all —
which is the point, since it lets a clean report still show its working.
Currently only the ``performance`` category populates these (its Core Web
Vitals and timing metrics); other categories send an empty list.

plan_name.title: Plan Name
plan_name.description: Display name of the plan, e.g. "Pro".

scans_used.title: Scans Used
scans_used.description: Scans created in the current calendar month (UTC).

scans_limit.title: Scans Limit
scans_limit.description: Scans the plan permits per calendar month.

scans_remaining.title: Scans Remaining
scans_remaining.description: Scans left before the monthly cap is reached.

period_start.title: Period Start
period_start.description: First instant of the current quota month (UTC).

categories.title: Categories
categories.description: Analysis categories this plan may run.

pdf_export.title: Pdf Export
pdf_export.description: Whether PDF report download is included.

public_api.title: Public Api
public_api.description: Whether API keys may be minted and used.

webhooks.title: Webhooks
webhooks.description: Whether a scan may request webhook delivery.

retention_days.title: Retention Days
retention_days.description: How long completed scans are kept.

scan_credits.title: Scan Credits
scan_credits.description: Unspent one-off scan credits. Each buys a single all-category scan outside the monthly quota, and is only spent on explicit request.

retention_grace_until.title: Retention Grace Until
retention_grace_until.description: When the extended retention granted after a plan downgrade ends. Until then scans are kept as though the account were still on its previous plan; after it, `retention_days` applies and older scans may be permanently deleted. Null when no grace period is running.

PlanUsageResponse.title: PlanUsageResponse
PlanUsageResponse.description:
The caller's plan entitlements and their usage against them (Phase 11 B3).

Exists because the limits were previously invisible: a user only discovered
the monthly cap by being 429'd. The SPA reads this to show remaining scans,
label the categories a plan withholds, and decide whether to offer an
upgrade prompt.

PortalResponse.title: PortalResponse
PortalResponse.description:
Short-lived authenticated links into Paddle's customer portal.

Minted per request and never stored — the token appended to each link is
temporary by design.

PublicConfigResponse.title: PublicConfigResponse
PublicConfigResponse.description: Runtime config the web UI reads on load.

PublicPlan.title: PublicPlan
PublicPlan.description:
One plan as the public pricing page renders it.

Deliberately a separate shape from :class:`PlanOption` rather than a loosened
one. That model serves the authenticated plan picker, where every entry is
buyable and every price is therefore non-null; this one has to carry **Free**,
which is the price anchor the pricing page is built around.

It also carries the Paddle price ids, which `PlanOption` has no reason to.
They are not secrets — a price id is a catalog pointer, and the client token
that dereferences it already ships via ``GET /api/v1/config`` — but they are
*configuration* (they differ between the sandbox and production catalogs),
which is why they come from the server rather than a `VITE_` build variable.
The browser needs them to ask Paddle for a localized, tax-inclusive price.

one_off_scan_paddle_price_id.title: One Off Scan Paddle Price Id

PublicPlansResponse.title: PublicPlansResponse
PublicPlansResponse.description: The full plan matrix, for the unauthenticated pricing page.

RecentDuplicateResponse.title: RecentDuplicateResponse
RecentDuplicateResponse.description:
Result of the pre-submit recent-duplicate check for GET /scans/recent-duplicate.

Advisory only — reports whether the caller scanned the same website within the
warning window so the UI can caution against tripping the site's WAF. It never
blocks submission.

email_notifications.title: Email Notifications
email_notifications.description: Send an email when a scan completes.

dark_mode.title: Dark Mode
dark_mode.description: Use the dark colour scheme in the web UI.

onboarding_dismissed.title: Onboarding Dismissed
onboarding_dismissed.description: Whether the user has dismissed the first-login onboarding walkthrough.

email.title: Email
email.description: Deprecated and rejected with 400. Changing an email address requires confirming the new one is reachable, so it goes through POST /auth/change-email instead.

secret.title: Secret
secret.description: The signing secret, as `whsec_<hex>`. Configure it in the receiver that verifies the `X-SyteCheck-Signature` header.

version.title: Version
version.description: Rotation counter. Rotating issues a new secret and immediately invalidates the previous one, so update the receiver first.

signature_max_age_seconds.title: Signature Max Age Seconds
signature_max_age_seconds.description: How old a signed timestamp may be before a receiver should reject the delivery as a replay.

WebhookSecretResponse.title: WebhookSecretResponse
WebhookSecretResponse.description:
An account's outbound webhook signing secret.

Returned in full on every read, unlike an API key, and the difference is
deliberate. A key is a *bearer* credential — anyone holding it can act as the
account, so it is stored hashed and shown once. This secret grants no access
to anything: it only lets the holder verify that a delivery came from us. The
cost of showing it again is therefore low, and the cost of *not* showing it is
high — a customer who loses it would otherwise have to rotate, breaking a
working integration to recover a value we can simply re-derive.
